clue.text: Censor correspondent, a contributor to comedy show

blocks.note: to censor someone is to silence them, to put a gag on them
a correspondent is someone who writes letters

explanation.surface: A censor and a newspaper correspondent both work on a television comedy programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pits a censor against a comic show, but the censor only supplies the verb for silencing, which is also a word for a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who supplies jokes and sketches for comedians is a gag writer, the everyday job title for such a scriptwriter.

clue.text: Angry sound from Greek member of parliament

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for Greek
a parliament is the collective noun for a group of owls, so one member of it is a single bird

explanation.surface: A Greek politician makes an angry noise in the chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member of parliament' begs to be MP; the trick is the collective noun, a parliament of owls, which makes the member a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A low rumbling noise made in the throat by a hostile dog or an irritated person expresses anger.

clue.text: Vulcan’s demise unexpectedly good news?

blocks.note: Vulcan is the Roman god of fire and the forge, so this is a god's, the apostrophe kept as a plain S
a demise is a death, an ending

explanation.surface: The setter, who signs as Vulcan, jokes that the news of their own death would be welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: Vulcan is also this setter's pseudonym, so the surface is a self-deprecating joke; in the wordplay he is simply the Roman god.
explanation.definitionFit: Something arriving as a stroke of luck exactly when needed is called heaven-sent, a gift from above.

clue.text: A measure of whisky not opened? It’s on the house

indicators.note: Something not opened has had its first part left shut, so the opening letter of the measure is dropped.

blocks.note: proof is the scale on which the alcoholic strength of spirits is measured
lose the first letter of the strength measure

explanation.surface: A pub landlord offers a free dram of whisky from an unopened bottle: it's on the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the house' is the pub phrase for free drinks, which fits the whisky; read literally it describes what sits on top of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: The covering that tops a building literally sits on the house, a playful literal reading of the idiom.

clue.text: Swell to maximum volume

blocks.note: taken as it stands
fortissimo, the musical marking for very loud, is written ff

explanation.surface: A sound engineer turns something up until it swells to full volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like a verb about sound rising; it is the old noun for a fashionable, upper-class man. A toff is a British term for a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal British terms for a smartly dressed person of wealth or high social class.

clue.text: Powerful preacher is on exam schedule

blocks.note: re means on the subject of, concerning
a viva is an oral examination, especially at a university
a schedule is a list of items or times

explanation.surface: A forceful preacher is named in the timetable for an examination.
explanation.walkthrough: A viva (short for viva voce) is the spoken exam a British student sits, often to defend a thesis.
explanation.definitionFit: An evangelist who holds rousing meetings to renew religious fervour in a community is a stirring, forceful speaker.

clue.text: No longer measure use of computers by youngster

blocks.note: a cub is a young animal, and a junior scout
information technology, the field of computers

explanation.surface: A child's time on computers should be measured no longer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' places the youngster beside the computers, and the youngster comes first. 'No longer' looks like 'stop'; here it means obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient unit of length based on the forearm, used in the Bible, is now obsolete and out of use.

clue.text: These days going into small business American is intrepid

indicators.note: One thing going into another ends up inside it, so the days sit within the firm and the American.

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
the present period is our age
the United States

explanation.surface: Starting a small business in America nowadays takes nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: The firm and the American join to make the outside, and 'these days' is read as a two-word phrase, our age, which slips in straight after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe someone brave, fearless and bold in the face of danger or difficulty.

clue.text: Airline gets one oaf to make emergency jump

blocks.note: British Airways
the Roman numeral
a lout is a clumsy, boorish person

explanation.surface: An airline takes on a clumsy passenger who has to leap from the plane in an emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: BA is the standard crossword abbreviation for British Airways.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilots leaving a crippled aircraft by parachute are said to do this, a fixed phrase for escaping by jumping.

clue.text: Beloved certain to walk round

indicators.note: Walking round something encircles it, so the word for walking wraps around the word for certain.

blocks.note: to tread is to walk or step
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A loved one is sure to take a stroll round the block.
explanation.walkthrough: The walking word splits after its fourth letter to take the certainty inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something held dear, cherished and highly valued is precious to its owner.

clue.text: Strange lad with pet, one a lot of money backed

definitions.text: one a lot of money backed

blocks.note: odd means strange
a boy, somebody's son
a teacher's pet is the favoured child

explanation.surface: An odd boy with his pet animal is somehow bankrolled by a large sum of money.
explanation.walkthrough: The joined letters regroup across the hyphen: the strange word and the lad read as a betting phrase, odds-on.
explanation.definitionFit: In horse racing, the runner priced at less than evens attracts the heaviest wagers from punters.

clue.text: Vegetable ship brought back

indicators.note: Something brought back returns the way it came, so the ship's part is read from its end.

blocks.note: the keel is the backbone along the bottom of a ship, standing for the whole vessel

explanation.surface: A cargo of vegetables is returned to port on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: A keel names the whole ship by one of its parts, a usage found in poetry ('keels' for ships).
explanation.definitionFit: A long green-and-white allium related to the onion, and the national emblem of Wales, is a garden vegetable.

clue.text: They fly around area by way of rocky peaks

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
via means by way of
a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor in south-west England

explanation.surface: Pilots take a route over an area of craggy mountain tops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' belongs with the definition, not the wordplay: no letters go around anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilots are people who operate aircraft, so they travel through the sky in planes.

clue.text: Believe spade for one to be plastic

blocks.note: to credit a story is to believe it
a spade is one example of a playing card

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to think of a garden spade as made of plastic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' reads as a material but is the everyday slang for paying by card.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, paying with plastic means paying by bank card, named for the material the cards are made of.

clue.text: Having cut back tree drench all around

indicators.note: Letters scattered all around are no longer in their order, so the tree and the soaking get rearranged.

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A gardener who has pruned a tree then soaks the ground all around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut back' suggests pruning, which suits the tree, but the definition is economic cost-cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm or government that has reduced its spending and economised is said to have made retrenchments.

clue.text: Submarine at first lacks rust protection

indicators.note: What comes at first is the opening, so only the leading letter of 'lacks' is used.

blocks.note: read as an adjective, submarine means beneath the sea
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A submarine has no protection against corrosion at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Submarine' looks like a noun, the vessel, but is used as the adjective. Underseal is the British word for the anti-rust coating on a car's underside.
explanation.definitionFit: A tar-like coating sprayed on a vehicle's underbody prevents corrosion of the chassis metal.

clue.text: Not recognised tossing and turning on new bunk

indicators.note: A restless sleeper tossing and turning keeps changing position, so the letters that follow move about.

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone lies sleepless, tossing and turning in a new bunk bed, unnoticed.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is exactly the restless sleep a new bunk would bring, so the surface hides it well.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening without anyone being aware of it is unknown, an old-fashioned form of that word.

clue.text: One consuming an apple

blocks.note: a person or animal that takes in food
an eating apple, sweet enough to eat raw rather than cook, is called one by growers

explanation.surface: Someone biting into an apple.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one idea, but it is two: a consumer, and the growers' word for a dessert apple, as opposed to a cooker.
explanation.definitionFit: A diner takes in food; separately, fruit growers call a sweet dessert variety, as against a cooking kind, by this name.

clue.text: Established pansy regularly in garden

indicators.note: Regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the flower is taken.
Put in the garden, the chosen letters sit inside the word for a flowerbed.

blocks.note: its second and fourth letters
a flowerbed is a patch of garden

explanation.surface: A pansy has taken root and become established in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of the flower go inside the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set up or located in a particular place, as a company headquartered somewhere, is said to be founded there.

clue.text: In a little less wind, let’s take someone for a ride

indicators.note: The answer lies within a small stretch of the words that follow, not in any one of them.

blocks.note: seven letters running from the end of the first word through the second into the third

explanation.surface: With the wind dropping a little, someone suggests taking a friend out for a drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let's' seems to belong to the invitation, but its first two letters complete the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone for a ride is an idiom for cheating or conning them out of money.

clue.text: Movingly describe united salvage effort

indicators.note: Done movingly, the letters are set in motion and change place.

blocks.note: taken as it stands
the standard abbreviation, as in football club names like Man U

explanation.surface: A reporter gives an emotional account of a joint recovery operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movingly' reads as 'with emotion' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt to save a failing company or a stricken vessel is a salvage operation, a recovery attempt.

clue.text: Septuagenarian perhaps eating large loaf

indicators.note: What is eaten goes inside the eater, so the pensioner takes in the size letter.

blocks.note: a baby boomer, born in the post-war birth surge, is typically now in their sixties or seventies
the clothing-size abbreviation

explanation.surface: An elderly person eats a big loaf of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' flags a septuagenarian as one example of the generation. A bloomer is a British crusty white loaf with diagonal slashes across the top.
explanation.definitionFit: A long rounded white bread with a slashed crust, common in British bakeries, is a kind of loaf.

clue.text: Domestic occupation for the woolly-minded?

blocks.note: the surface reading: people whose thinking is vague and muddled
the setter's reading: people whose minds are on yarn, keen on working with it

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark licenses reading 'woolly-minded' literally: thinking about wool rather than thinking foggily.
explanation.definitionFit: A home craft making garments from yarn with two needles is a pastime for those devoted to fibre.

clue.text: School class in shape for months

indicators.note: The word sits in the phrase after it, spread over two neighbouring words.

blocks.note: the whole first word plus the opening letter of the second

explanation.surface: A school class has been keeping fit for months.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes to one word: a British school year group, a synonym for shape, and the letters inside the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools a year group or class is traditionally called this, and the word also means outline or configuration.

clue.text: Old Testament figure who took the tablets as directed

definitions.text: Old Testament figure who took the tablets as directed

blocks.note: the surface reading: swallowed pills following the dosage on the medicine label
the setter's reading: the prophet who carried the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments down Mount Sinai as God instructed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tablets' and 'as directed' are pharmacy language, but the tablets are stone and the direction came from God.
explanation.definitionFit: The Exodus leader received the commandments carved on stone slabs and brought them down to the Israelites.

clue.text: Inconclusive game that attracts a crowd

blocks.note: a match ending level, with no winner
a star turn or attraction that pulls people in

explanation.surface: A tied match that still brings in a big audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs the two meanings together as one football fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: A tied contest is a draw, and a popular performer or event that pulls in spectators is also called one.

clue.text: Not many heard this sigh of relief

indicators.note: What is heard is taken by ear, so the word for not many counts by its sound.

blocks.note: a small number, which is said the same as the exhalation

explanation.surface: Only a handful of people heard someone sigh with relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' points the definition at the answer itself: the answer is the sound of the sigh.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of relief, the noise of breath let out after a narrow escape, is written as this interjection.

clue.text: Roller making its way through London in song

definitions.text: Roller making its way through London in song

blocks.clueFragment: Roller making its way through London
blocks.note: the surface reading: a Rolls-Royce car, or a steamroller, driving through the capital
the setter's reading: a song whose chorus says the river keeps rolling along, so the river is the roller

explanation.walkthrough: 'Roller' suggests a car or a wave; the 1930s song says the river 'keeps rolling along', and the Thames is London's river.
explanation.definitionFit: The personified river through the capital is the subject of a well-known popular song that says it keeps rolling along.

clue.text: Very much unfinished

blocks.note: an informal intensifier, as when a gift is said to please someone enormously
something without a conclusion lacks its last part

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is a colloquial adverb; the second is taken literally, a thing with nothing to close it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means enormously or a great deal, and literally something lacking a conclusion is incomplete.

clue.text: The way to get to the bottom of things

definitions.text: The way to get to the bottom of things

blocks.clueFragment: get to the bottom of things
blocks.note: the surface reading: to investigate a mystery and find out what really happened
the setter's reading: a direction of travel that ends at the lowest point of whatever you are on

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for investigating is read literally: the route to the lowest part of anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving towards a lower level or place is the direction that reaches the base of an object.
